# Psalm 118: Verse-by-Verse Research Notes

**Before you use these notes:** I ran out of search and page-read limits before I could cover all three parts of your request. Enduring Word's page also cut off partway through verse 17, so for verses 19–29 I'm using the summary text that came back from the search, not the full page. These are the gaps:
- **Not found:** netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, any Orthodox site (oca.org), catholic.com, and any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm. Nothing below covers those.
- **No traditions clearly clashing:** I found no verse where Protestant traditions disagree on doctrine. The nearest thing is the spread of views on what "the day" means in v. 24.
- **Lutheran view:** this comes only through Luther as quoted by Enduring Word. I didn't reach lcms.org or 1517.org.

## Background (whole psalm)
- Guzik (Enduring Word) thinks David probably wrote it. He notes that "His mercy endures forever" appears 34 times throughout the psalms as a liturgical call-and-response. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Guzik also says it was the last of the six "Egyptian Hallel" psalms sung at Passover. So the hymn Jesus sang at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30) refers to these psalms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Guzik says the Talmud records the psalm also being sung at the Feast of Tabernacles (VanGemeren cited). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- On the setting, Spurgeon would refer it to no one incident in particular, but to regard it as a national song, adapted alike for the rise of a chosen here, and the building of a temple. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps118.cfm
- Bible Hub's study notes give two possible settings. Early Jewish tradition linked it to King David's restoration after conflict, while others hear post-exile voices—fresh from Babylon—celebrating the rebuilt temple. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/118.htm
- Clarke (Methodist) describes Bishop Horsley's view that the psalm is a procession sung in parts. A conqueror and his followers arrive at the temple gate and priests answer from inside. Horsley saw the conqueror as Messiah and his followers as the redeemed. Clarke himself thought this "too mechanical." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- Luther, as quoted by Guzik, called this his own beloved psalm, one that helped him out of many great troubles when rulers and scholars could not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/

## Verse notes

**v. 1:** Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): God is to be thanked because goodness is his very nature, not only because he does us good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Guzik: "loving devotion" translates *hesed*, God's loyal covenant love, which will never be taken from his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Spurgeon: mercy is a great part of his goodness, and one which more concerns us than any other, for we are sinners and have need of his mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps118.cfm

**vv. 2–4:** Guzik, quoting Maclaren: three groups are called on, the whole nation, the priests, and "those who fear the LORD," meaning Gentiles who had come to Israel's God. This suggests different parts of the congregation sang different lines. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Spurgeon: believing God's goodness isn't enough; we must declare the goodness of God; truth is not to be hushed up, but proclaimed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps118.cfm
- Matthew Henry: the thanks of everyone who truly fears the Lord please God as much as those of Israel or the priests. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm

**v. 3:** Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): if David wrote it, the priests had special reason for thanks, since Saul had massacred many of them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Clarke: the priesthood was still preserved and temple worship restored. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 4:** Clarke takes "those who fear the LORD" to mean all sincere penitents and true believers. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 5:** Guzik: God answered by setting the psalmist in a secure, "broad place" (NKJV wording). He also quotes Luther urging the troubled to get on their knees and pray rather than brood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Matthew Henry: David liked to remember his former low state instead of forgetting it once God had lifted him up. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm

**v. 6:** Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): the psalmist doesn't say he won't suffer, only that he won't fear, because God's favour far outweighs people's hatred. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/

**v. 7:** Guzik compares Romans 8:31, "If God is for us, who can be against us?" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Clarke's literal reading: "The Lord is to me among my helpers." He takes the second half as "I shall look among them that hate me," meaning he can face them all and will see them defeated. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- Augustine (Catholic reading; his Latin Bible numbers this Psalm 117) applies "enemies" to the number of evil men, or from the number of evil angels. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801118.htm

**vv. 8–9:** Guzik lists Spurgeon's reasons trusting God is better (wiser, morally right, safer, and so on). He also passes on Boice's report that these are the middle verses of the Bible by verse count. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Clarke: princes often *cannot* deliver, and often *will not* when they can. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- An old saying quoted by Spurgeon: Great men's words, saith one, are like dead men's shoes; he may go barefoot that waiteth for them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps118.cfm

**vv. 10–12:** Clarke gives two historical options: neighbouring nations resisting David early in his reign, or the Samaritans and others opposing the rebuilding after the exile. He also lists other renderings of "cut them off" ("disappoint," "repel," "avenged"). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- Matthew Henry: the repeated "surrounded me" shows the enemies were fierce, and kept regrouping after setbacks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Kidner on v. 12: a fire of thorns burns out as quickly as it flares, and so evil's power will be short-lived. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/

**v. 13:** Clarke: whatever skill and courage the psalmist had, he gives God the glory for the victory. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 14:** Guzik: this quotes the song of the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 15). The point is to seek God himself rather than the gifts of strength, song and salvation apart from him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/

**vv. 15–16:** Guzik: the "right hand" is the hand of skill and strength, repeated for emphasis. Maclaren (quoted) suggests "tents" may hint at the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Clarke: where before there was only wailing, now everyone rejoices at the deliverance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 17:** Guzik: the psalmist was sure God would keep him from death in this crisis. Jesus, singing it the night before the cross, could say it knowing death would not hold him. Guzik adds, citing Spurgeon, that Luther had this verse written on his study wall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Matthew Henry: life is only worth living to declare God's works. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm

**v. 18:** Guzik: God's discipline had a training purpose and would benefit the psalmist rather than destroy him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-118.cfm
- Matthew Henry: when we are disciplined severely we shouldn't despair of life. He applies the verse to Christ, whom God did not leave in the grave. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm

**vv. 19–20:** Guzik: the psalmist probably pictured a victory procession entering the holy city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Clarke: v. 19 is the king asking for the temple doors to be opened, and v. 20 is the Levites' reply. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 21:** Clarke: he is now inside the gates and bursts into thanks, because God himself has saved him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 22:** Guzik: this verse is quoted more in the New Testament than any other Old Testament verse. The religious leaders ("the builders") rejected Jesus, but God made him the cornerstone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Got Questions: Jesus quoted it about his own rejection, and Peter took up the theme (Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:6–8). https://www.gotquestions.org/this-is-the-day-that-the-Lord-has-made.html
- Clarke: it must have been a proverb, and the most enlightened Jewish teachers read it as a prophecy of the Messiah. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- Augustine (Catholic): Christ became the cornerstone to make in Himself of two one new man, uniting Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:15–16). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801118.htm
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the gospels quote this verse from the Greek Septuagint, not the Hebrew. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11460a.htm

**v. 23:** Augustine: Christ would not have become the cornerstone without suffering, yet He became not this through those from whom He suffered. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801118.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ's humbling and his exaltation were both God's work (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm
- Guzik: only the Father could lift Jesus up. Leaders, crowds and disciples all failed him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/

**v. 24 (the most debated verse in these sources):**
- *Context first:* In context, Psalm 118:24 refers not to every day, but to a particular, momentous day: the day when the Lord made the rejected stone the cornerstone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_118:24_commentary
- *David's coronation:* Calvin (Reformed) took it as the happy day David was finally made king over Israel. Coffman reads it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/118-24.html
- *A day spared from death:* Barnes (Presbyterian) saw it as an extra day the writer never expected to live to see. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/118-24.html
- *The resurrection:* Clarke (Methodist) said it was "without doubt" the day of the resurrection. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html Spurgeon (Baptist) said the day of David's enthronement was a turning point, but in a far higher sense the day of our Lord's resurrection is a new day of God's own making. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_118:24_commentary
- *The triumphal entry:* Guzik (Calvary Chapel, listed under Pentecostal/charismatic in your site list) says the day was the day Jesus entered Jerusalem with hosannas welcoming Him as Israel's Savior. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- *The whole gospel age, and Sunday:* Matthew Henry sees it as the whole time of the gospel, the "day of salvation." Elsewhere he says Sabbath days should be days of rejoicing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/118-24.html https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/118-24.htm Ironside linked it to Christians honouring the day of Christ's resurrection. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_118:24_commentary
- *A future kingdom:* John Butler (quoted on Precept Austin) points ahead to the day He will rule the world and Israel will be the great nation of the world. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_118:24_commentary
- *The popular "every day" use:* Craig Keener (on Precept Austin) says the idea that God made every day is true, but other verses prove it better. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61903/ Bible Hub's study notes allow both: the verse points mainly to the cornerstone day and the resurrection, but the principle applies to each new day God grants. https://biblehub.com/psalms/118-24.htm
- *Early church (Catholic/patristic):* Augustine read it as a prophetic day not visible to physical eyes, one that has a dawn but never a sunset, introduced by the cornerstone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61903/

**v. 25:** Clarke: the Hebrew *hoshiah nna* ("save, we pray") gives us "hosanna." It was sung at the Feast of Tabernacles with green branches in hand, and the children sang it when Christ entered Jerusalem. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- J. Vernon McGee says the same about the hosanna cry at the triumphal entry. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_118:24_commentary

**v. 26:** Got Questions: the crowds quoted this verse at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9). https://www.gotquestions.org/this-is-the-day-that-the-Lord-has-made.html
- Guzik: the same deliverer welcomed with open gates, hosannas and blessings was the stone that would be rejected. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Clarke: "we bless you" is the Levites answering the king. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html

**v. 27:** Clarke:
- "God" here is *El Yehovah*, "the strong God Jehovah." The light might have been a divine splendour shining on the procession.
- The Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) attributes "bind the sacrifice" to Samuel.
- The Vulgate and Septuagint read it as "keep the festival with thick boughs."
- Applied to us, it means to give thanks and meet in church to celebrate.

https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- Guzik: Jesus sang this line hours before the cross, essentially inviting the Father to bind Him to the cross as the final, perfect sacrifice. For us, it means binding ourselves as living sacrifices. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-118/
- Augustine: the one who came in the Lord's name and gave light is Christ, who is God, He is equal with the Father. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801118.htm

**v. 28:** Clarke: "you are my God" means "I have taken you for my portion," and the repetition shows how eager he is to express his gratitude. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-118.html
- Spurgeon: in the procession reading, the conqueror sings this verse alone before the closing chorus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps118.cfm

**v. 29:** Guzik: the psalm ends where it began. If we start with praise, we are in a better position to end with praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-118.cfm
- Matthew Henry: in Christ, God is good to us and his mercy lasts forever, and in Christ the covenant of grace is made secure. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_118.cfm
